```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse   = TRUE,
  comment    = "#>",
  fig.width  = 6,
  fig.height = 4
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(rscprep)
```

A barcode rank plot is the first thing to look at when a sample comes back
with an unexpected cell count. It plots total UMI count against barcode rank
on log-log axes: a sharp cliff between a plateau of real cells and a long
tail of empty droplets means cell calling had an easy decision to make, and a
shallow gradual slope means it did not.

`plotBarcodeRanks()` draws that plot. This vignette covers the simplest case
-- one biological sample per GEM well, nothing multiplexed, where each curve
describes exactly one sample and needs no caveats.

`DropletUtils` does the ranking and is a `Suggests`, not an `Imports`, so
install it before you start:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
BiocManager::install(c("DropletUtils", "S4Vectors"))
```

```{r, child = "_heart1k.Rmd"}
```

The bundled raw matrix drops every barcode that had fewer than 25 UMIs in the
original run. After the gene subset those barcodes total as little as 9, so
the curves below stop near 10 on the y-axis; a full raw matrix runs down to 1.

## One sample

```{r one-sample}
ranks <- plotBarcodeRanks(
  path  = outs,
  multi = FALSE
)

ranks$heart_1k_v3$plot
```

`path` is the same `outs/` directory you would hand `seuratFrom10x()`, and
the sample is named the same way (after the folder above `outs`). What
differs is which file gets read.

## Why this reads a different file

Cell calling is exactly the step that separates the raw matrix from the
filtered one. The filtered matrix has already had the empty droplets removed,
so the left-hand cliff (the thing the plot exists to show you) is gone
before you start. `plotBarcodeRanks()` therefore reads the **raw** matrix:

| | `seuratFrom10x()` | `plotBarcodeRanks()` |
|---|---|---|
| Reads | `outs/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5` | `outs/raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5` |
| Contains | barcodes called as cells | every barcode in the GEM well |
| Order | 10^3 to 10^4 columns | 10^5 to 10^6 columns (20,650 in the bundled copy) |

Nothing is filtered by this function. The knee and the inflection are drawn
so you can compare them against what Cell Ranger actually kept; neither is a
threshold applied to anything.

## "Unpooled" has two shapes

The distinction that matters for reading these curves is whether the GEM well
held one sample or several.

```{r unpooled-shapes, eval = FALSE}
# A `cellranger count` run
plotBarcodeRanks(path = "/path/to/Sample_1/outs", multi = FALSE)

# A singleplex Flex or 5' run, processed with `cellranger multi`
plotBarcodeRanks(path = "/path/to/Sample_2/outs", multi = TRUE)
```

Both are unpooled, and both give you one curve for one sample. Set `multi` to
match the pipeline that wrote the directory, not to whether anything was
multiplexed: `cellranger multi` writes `per_sample_outs/` even when it
demultiplexed exactly one sample, and the raw matrix moves with it:

| `multi` | Raw matrix location |
|---|---|
| `FALSE` | `outs/raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5` |
| `TRUE` | `outs/multi/count/raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5` |

If your `cellranger multi` output has been staged or flattened and the raw
matrix sits directly in `outs/`, that is checked as a fallback, so both
layouts resolve either way. `$h5` on the result records which file was
actually read.

The reason this is worth being careful about: for a genuinely pooled run,
`cellranger multi` writes **one** run-level raw matrix shared by every demuxed
sample, because cell calling happens once per GEM well and only afterwards are
barcodes assigned to samples. So a pool gives you one curve describing the
pool, not one curve per sample. When the well held a single sample, that
run-level matrix *is* that sample's matrix and the caveat disappears, which
is why this vignette can treat both rows above the same way.

## A batch of samples

Same manifest `seuratFrom10x()` takes, so one table drives both halves of the
workflow. The bundled data is one sample, so this example uses placeholder
paths and is not run:

```{r manifest, eval = FALSE}
manifest <- data.frame(
  Path = c(
    "/path/to/Sample_1/outs",
    "/path/to/Sample_2/outs",
    "/path/to/Sample_3/outs"
  ),
  multi = FALSE
)

ranks <- plotBarcodeRanks(manifest = manifest)

names(ranks)
#> [1] "Sample_1" "Sample_2" "Sample_3"
```

Runs are processed strictly one at a time -- read, ranked, reduced to a
curve, released -- so peak memory is set by your largest single sample rather
than by the length of the manifest. That matters here more than it looks: a
raw matrix has a column for every barcode in the well, and holding a dozen of
them at once is what makes this kind of loop fall over.

## What comes back

One element per sample, each a list:

```{r result}
heart <- ranks$heart_1k_v3

head(heart$data)            # the plotted curve
heart$knee                  # optimistic cutoff, in UMIs
heart$inflection            # permissive cutoff, in UMIs
heart$n_barcodes            # barcodes in the raw matrix
heart$n_above_inflection    # roughly, the cells you would expect
basename(heart$h5)          # the file this was computed from
```

`heart$plot` is the ggplot2 object drawn above. Nothing was printed or saved
until it was asked for.

`data` is the curve, not the raw matrix: zero-count barcodes are dropped
(they have no place on a log axis, and in a raw matrix they are the clear
majority) and barcodes tying on total are collapsed to one row, since they
share a rank and plot at one point anyway. That turns millions of rows into a
few thousand -- small enough to write to CSV, which the full per-barcode table
is not.

## The check this is actually for

`n_above_inflection` is a rough expected cell count derived independently of
Cell Ranger's cell caller. Comparing it against what the filtered matrix
actually kept is the whole point of drawing these:

```{r crosscheck}
# min.cells / min.features off, so `called` is what Cell Ranger kept
seurat_list <- seuratFrom10x(path = outs, multi = FALSE,
                             min.cells = 0, min.features = 0)

data.frame(
  expected = vapply(ranks, function(x) x$n_above_inflection, numeric(1)),
  called   = vapply(seurat_list, ncol, integer(1))
)
```

The two agree closely, which is what a clean run looks like: the curve has a
sharp cliff, and Cell Ranger's cell caller and the inflection point found
nearly the same edge. A sample where they disagree badly is the signal to go
look at its curve. A shallow slope with no clear cliff usually means ambient
RNA, low viability, or a wetting failure, and the called cell count from that
sample should be treated with suspicion regardless of which side of the
discrepancy you believe.

## Writing figures out

```{r outdir}
outdir <- file.path(tempdir(), "barcode_ranks")
ranks  <- plotBarcodeRanks(path = outs, multi = FALSE, outdir = outdir)

list.files(outdir)
```

Writes `<sample>_barcode_ranks.csv` and `<sample>_barcode_ranks.png` per
sample, creating the directory if needed, and still returns everything in
memory. Sample names come from directory names, so any character that is not
safe in a filename is replaced with `_` in the file stem only -- the list
names are left alone. `width`, `height` and `dpi` are passed through to
`ggplot2::ggsave()`.

## Tuning the fit

`lower` is the total UMI count at or below which a barcode is assumed empty.
It sets the ambient profile and bounds the spline fit; it does **not** filter
the curve, and barcodes below it are still plotted.

```{r lower}
plotBarcodeRanks(path = outs, multi = FALSE, lower = 500)$heart_1k_v3$plot
```

Anything else goes to `DropletUtils::barcodeRanks()`:

```{r dots, results = "hide"}
plotBarcodeRanks(
  path         = outs,
  multi        = FALSE,
  lower        = 100,
  fit.bounds   = NULL,
  exclude.from = 50,
  df           = 20
)
```

Raise `df` for a stiffer spline if the fitted line is chasing noise in the
tail; `exclude.from` drops the highest-ranked barcodes from the fit, which
helps when a handful of enormous barcodes drag the knee upward.

## Changing the figure

The plots are plain ggplots, so nothing is locked in:

```{r customise}
library(ggplot2)

ranks$heart_1k_v3$plot +
  labs(subtitle = "E18 mouse heart, 10x demo run") +
  theme_prepro("clean")
```

And `data` is a plain data frame, so a single figure across every sample is
one `rbind` away. With several samples in `ranks` (one here, so this is not
run):

```{r facet, eval = FALSE}
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ranks), function(s) {
  cbind(Sample = s, ranks[[s]]$data)
}))

ggplot(curves, aes(rank, total, colour = Sample)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_prepro() +
  labs(x = "Barcode rank", y = "Total UMI count") +
  theme_prepro("airy")
```

Overlaying samples this way is usually more informative than reading the
per-sample figures side by side -- a curve that sits below the others, or
turns over earlier, stands out immediately.

## When a sample fails

Two things can go wrong per sample: the raw matrix is missing, or
`barcodeRanks()` cannot fit a curve to it. Both follow the same rule as
`seuratFrom10x()`.

In manifest mode the sample is skipped with a warning and the rest of the
batch still runs, so the returned list can be shorter than the manifest:

```{r partial}
# the bundled sample, plus a run whose outs/ was never copied over
manifest <- data.frame(
  Path  = c(outs, file.path(tempdir(), "Sample_2", "outs")),
  multi = FALSE
)

ranks <- plotBarcodeRanks(manifest = manifest)

setdiff(basename(dirname(manifest$Path)), names(ranks))
```

In `path` mode the same condition is an error instead -- there is no other
sample to fall back on, so failing quietly would leave you with an empty
list and no explanation.

If the raw matrix is genuinely absent, the usual cause is that only the
filtered outputs were copied off the sequencing core's storage.
`raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5` is large and often gets left behind; there is no
way to reconstruct it from what you have, so it has to be fetched.

## Getting the matrices themselves

`plotBarcodeRanks()` never hands you a raw matrix -- it reads each one, ranks
it, and drops it. If you want the matrices, `rawMatrixFrom10x()` takes the
same arguments and returns them, with no such promise about memory:

```{r raw}
raw <- rawMatrixFrom10x(path = outs, multi = FALSE)

dim(raw$heart_1k_v3)

range(Matrix::colSums(raw$heart_1k_v3))
```

The original raw matrix had 6,794,880 barcodes. The bundled copy keeps the
20,650 that had at least 25 UMIs before the gene subset.

It returns count matrices rather than Seurat objects on purpose. Wrapping a
raw matrix in a Seurat object means computing per-cell metadata for hundreds
of thousands of droplets that are about to be discarded, and barcode ranking
only ever needs the column sums.
